newsitem.title: USA: Defense witness says bomber may have died in blast.
newsitem.headline: Defense witness says bomber may have died in blast.

text.p: Lawyers for accused bomber Timothy McVeigh started their defence on Thursday, suggesting that a never-identified leg found in the Oklahoma City federal building explosion belonged to the actual bomber.
A British forensic scientist, testifying for the defence, said the unidentified leg could have belonged to the bomber.
Dr. Thomas Marshall, a retired Northern Ireland pathologist, said it was possible for people very close to explosions to be completely blown to pieces, except for a single body part.

"To be disintegrated so completely you have to be near the bomb," Marshall testified at the trial in which McVeigh is accused of the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people.

He was one of the witnesses called on the first day of the defence's case. The prosecution rested its case on Wednesday after calling 137 witnesses who built a web of circumstantial evidence against the Gulf War Veteran who has pleaded not guilty but faces the death penalty if convicted.
Marshall's testimony supported a defence theory that the real bomber had not been identified and that the unidentified leg found could very well belong to that person.

Marshall said experience of conducting autopsies on bomb victims in Northern Ireland taught him that people usually come forward to identify bombing victims. "When nobody misses them, it reinforces the suggestion the deceased is involved in the bombing," Marshall said.
He said a limb that has not been tied to any known victims of the bombing was "an extra left leg. Until shown otherwise, this must be an extra victim -- a 169th victim."
In earlier defence testimony, the medical examiner for the state of Oklahoma testified that the extra left leg found at the blast had never been identified.
After the bombing, the FBI launched a nationwide manhunt for a "John Doe No. 2," but never found him.

Another defence witness, a deliveryman for a Chinese restaurant, Jeff Davis, testfied he brought food to the motel room the prosecution claims McVeigh used in the days before the bombing. But Davis said the man he delivered the food to was not McVeigh and that there was no one else in the motel room at the time.
Despite a vigorous cross-examination from prosecutor Larry Mackey, Davis held to his account, insisting the man was not McVeigh.
The defence also tried to create doubt about testimony that linked the Ryder truck used in the blast to McVeigh.
Two defence witnesses said three days before the bombing they saw a Ryder truck at the Junction City, Kansas, motel where McVeigh is believed to have stayed.
The prosecution maintains McVeigh did not rent the truck until the following day, a Monday.
Witnesses Herta King and Renda Truong told the court they were sure about the day because it was Easter Sunday, April 16, 1995.
"There's no question in my mind. It was Easter Sunday," King said. She had stopped by the Dreamland Motel to leave an Easter basket for her son who was staying there.
The prosecution has previously presented a witness who identified McVeigh as the man who rented the truck on Monday, April 17, two days before the bombing.
Using an axle found near the blast site, investigators traced the truck to a Ryder rental depot in Junction City.
However, both defence witnesses remembered the size of the Ryder truck differently.

Truong, a high school student who was a friend of the motel owner's daughter, said it was a 20-foot (6-metre) truck, while King, who testified that she had previously rented a Ryder truck, said it was not the 20-foot size.
Both women said they did not see McVeigh at the motel.
